units.title: Exploring One-Variable Data
units.kid: Looking at one list of numbers
units.summary: Statistics starts with a list of [[data]]. In this unit you learn to draw it, find its middle, and see how spread out it is.
units.example: Your class writes down how many minutes each kid reads at night. A [[histogram]] shows most kids read 20 to 30 minutes, and one kid reads 120. That kid is an [[outlier]].
ideas: Is it a [[categorical|category]] or a [[quantitative|number]]? That decides the graph: bar charts for categories; [[histogram|histograms]], dotplots and [[boxplot|boxplots]] for numbers.
Always describe four things, in the story's words: shape, outliers, center and spread. A memory trick: SOCS.
Center: the [[mean]] is the average and the [[median]] is the middle. If the data is [[skewed]], the mean gets pulled toward the long tail.
Spread: [[sd|standard deviation]] goes with the mean, and [[iqr|IQR]] goes with the median.
A [[zscore|z-score]] says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean, so you can compare things on different scales.
Lots of shapes are close to the [[normal|normal curve]]. Use the [[empirical|68–95–99.7 rule]] for quick estimates.
units.watch: Don't just list numbers. Say what they mean in the story: "The median reading time is 25 minutes," not just "median = 25."
units.ask: What's the difference between mean and median, and when should I use each one?

units.title: Exploring Two-Variable Data
units.summary: Now you look at two things at once, like hours of sleep and test scores, to see if they move together.
units.example: Plot hours studied against test score. The dots climb up and to the right in a fairly straight line, so there's a strong, positive relationship.
ideas: Two categories? Use a two-way table and compare percents, not raw counts.
Two numbers? Make a [[scatterplot]] and describe direction, form, strength and unusual points.
[[correlation|Correlation (r)]] runs from −1 to 1. Near ±1 is strong; near 0 is weak. It only measures straight-line patterns.
The [[lsrl|regression line]] ŷ = a + bx predicts y. Explain the [[slope]] in context: "for each extra hour, the predicted score goes up b points."
A [[residual]] is actual minus predicted. A residual plot with no pattern means a straight line is a good fit.
[[r2|r²]] tells you what percent of the change in y the line explains.
units.watch: Correlation is not causation. Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but ice cream doesn't cause sunburns. Hot weather causes both.
units.ask: How do I explain the slope of a regression line in context?

units.title: Collecting Data
units.summary: Bad data gives bad answers, no matter how good your math is. This unit is about picking fair samples and running fair experiments.
units.example: To learn what your school thinks of lunch, you could ask only your friends (unfair) or pick 50 random student ID numbers (fair).
ideas: The [[population]] is everyone you care about. The [[sample]] is who you actually ask.
Random ways to sample: [[srs|simple random sample]], [[stratified|stratified]], [[cluster|cluster]] and systematic.
[[bias|Bias]] sneaks in through convenience samples, voluntary response (only people who care answer), undercoverage, nonresponse and leading questions.
An [[observational|observational study]] only watches. An [[experiment]] gives [[treatment|treatments]].
Good experiments have comparison (a [[control|control group]]), [[randomassign|random assignment]], enough subjects, and the same conditions for everyone. [[blinding|Blinding]] helps too.
Random sampling lets you talk about the whole population. Random assignment lets you talk about cause and effect.
units.watch: Random sampling and random assignment do different jobs. Sampling is about WHO is in the study. Assignment is about WHICH treatment each person gets.
units.ask: What's the difference between random sampling and random assignment?

units.title: Probability, Random Variables, and Probability Distributions
units.summary: [[probability|Probability]] is the math of chance. You'll work out how likely things are and what happens on average in the long run.
units.example: A spinner is one-quarter red. Spin it 1,000 times and about 250 spins land on red. That's the [[lawlarge|law of large numbers]].
ideas: A probability is between 0 and 1, and all the possible outcomes add up to 1.
"Or" rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B). "And" rule for [[independent]] events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).
[[conditional|Conditional probability]]: P(A | B) = P(A and B) ÷ P(B). Two-way tables and tree diagrams make these easier.
A [[randomvar|random variable]] has an [[expected|expected value]] (its long-run average) and a standard deviation.
[[binomial|Binomial]]: a set number of tries, count the successes. [[geometric|Geometric]]: count the tries until the first success.
Combining independent random variables: means add, and variances (SD²) add. Even when you subtract, the variances still add.
units.watch: [[mutex|Mutually exclusive]] is not the same as independent. If two things can't happen together, knowing one happened changes the chance of the other a lot.
units.ask: How do I know if a problem is binomial or geometric?

units.title: Sampling Distributions
units.summary: Every sample gives a slightly different answer. This unit shows how much answers wobble, so you can trust them the right amount.
units.example: Five classes each ask 30 random students if they like pizza best. They get 55%, 61%, 58%, 52% and 60%. None is exactly right, but they cluster around the truth.
ideas: A [[parameter]] describes the population and is usually unknown. A [[statistic]] comes from a sample.
A [[samplingdist|sampling distribution]] shows all the values a statistic could take across many samples.
Bigger samples wobble less. The spread shrinks with √n, so four times the sample size cuts the [[standarderror|standard error]] in half.
For proportions: the center is p and the SD is √(p(1 − p)/n). It's about normal when np ≥ 10 and n(1 − p) ≥ 10.
For means: the center is μ and the SD is σ/√n. The [[clt|central limit theorem]] says it's about normal when n ≥ 30.
A good statistic is [[unbiased]] (centered on the truth) and has low variability.
units.watch: The central limit theorem is about the shape of the sample MEANS, not the shape of one sample or of the population.
units.ask: Can you explain the central limit theorem like I'm 10?

units.title: Inference for Categorical Data: Proportions
units.kid: Guessing a percent from a sample
units.summary: Now you use a sample to say something about everyone, like "about 58% of all students want school to start later."
units.example: In a random sample of 200 students, 116 (58%) want a later start. A 95% [[ci|confidence interval]] says the true percent is probably between 51% and 65%.
ideas: A confidence interval is estimate ± [[marginoferror|margin of error]]. For a proportion: p̂ ± z*·√(p̂(1 − p̂)/n).
The [[confidencelevel|confidence level]] (like 95%) is about the method: 95% of intervals made this way catch the truth.
A significance test asks "could this just be luck?" Start with [[hypothesis|hypotheses]]: H₀: p = p₀ against Hₐ: p > p₀, p < p₀ or p ≠ p₀.
The [[pvalue|p-value]] is the chance of results this extreme if H₀ were true. If the p-value is below [[alpha|α]], reject H₀.
Mistakes happen: a [[type1|Type I error]] is a false alarm and a [[type2|Type II error]] is a missed alarm.
Always check the [[conditions]]: Random, 10%, and Large counts (at least 10 successes and 10 failures).
units.watch: Don't say "there's a 95% chance the true value is in my interval." Say "We are 95% confident the interval from __ to __ captures the true proportion of __."
units.ask: What does a p-value actually mean?

units.title: Inference for Quantitative Data: Means
units.kid: Guessing an average from a sample
units.summary: The same big ideas as Unit 6, but for averages. Because we don't know σ, we use the [[tdist|t-distribution]] instead of z.
units.example: A random sample of 25 batteries lasts 9.6 hours on average. The box says 10 hours. A t-test tells you if 9.6 is too low to blame on luck.
ideas: Use t, not z, for means: x̄ ± t*·s/√n, with [[df|df]] = n − 1.
Normal condition: n ≥ 30, OR the population is normal, OR a graph of the sample shows no strong skew or outliers.
One sample, two separate samples, or [[paired|paired data]]? Pick the matching test.
For paired data (before and after on the same people), subtract to get one list of differences, then do a one-sample t on those differences.
Bigger samples and less variation make intervals narrower and tests more [[power|powerful]].
units.watch: Two lists from the same people (before and after) is paired, not two-sample. Ask: is each number in list 1 linked to one number in list 2?
units.ask: How do I tell paired data from two independent samples?

units.title: Inference for Categorical Data: Chi-Square
units.summary: Chi-square tests check whether counts in categories match what you'd expect, or whether two category variables are linked.
units.example: A candy bag should be 20% each of five colors. You count 100 candies and get 30 red. A chi-square test checks if that's too far off to be luck.
ideas: [[chisquare|χ²]] = Σ (observed − expected)² ÷ expected. A bigger χ² means a worse fit.
Goodness of fit: one variable compared to a claimed distribution. df = number of categories − 1.
Independence (one sample, two variables) or homogeneity (several groups, one variable): use a two-way table, with df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
[[expectedcounts|Expected counts]] in a two-way table: (row total × column total) ÷ grand total.
Conditions: Random, 10%, and every expected count at least 5.
units.watch: Check "at least 5" with the expected counts, not the observed ones.
units.ask: When do I use chi-square goodness of fit vs independence?

units.title: Inference for Quantitative Data: Slopes
units.summary: A regression line from a sample might show a slope just by luck. This unit tests whether the true slope is really different from zero.
units.example: In a sample of 20 kids, more screen time goes with less sleep (slope −0.4). Is there a real link for all kids, or could the true slope be 0?
ideas: The sample [[slope]] b estimates the true slope β.
Hypotheses: H₀: β = 0 (no straight-line relationship) against Hₐ: β ≠ 0, β > 0 or β < 0.
Interval: b ± t*·SE_b, with df = n − 2. Computer output usually gives you b and SE_b.
[[teststat|Test statistic]]: t = b ÷ SE_b.
Conditions (LINER): Linear, Independent, Normal residuals, Equal spread of residuals, Random.
units.watch: Read computer output carefully: the slope is the "Coef" next to the x variable, not the one next to "Constant."
units.ask: How do I read regression computer output on the AP exam?
